title: The Missing Multiplicative Recurrence
content: The parent entry combinations-formula-oq-02 proves the additive Catalan identity Cₙ·(n+1) = C(2n,n), the 4ⁿ growth bounds, monotonicity, and the convolution recurrence. Its header also advertises a third, MULTIPLICATIVE recurrence — Segner's ratio recurrence C_{n+1} = (2(2n+1)/(n+2))·Cₙ — but never proves it. This entry supplies that proof and the sharp two-sided growth bounds it yields, all verified and axiom-free. The multiplicative recurrence is the efficient way to compute Catalan numbers (no factorials, no subtraction, no convolution sum) and it pins the growth rate between 2 and 4 per step.
mathContext: Integer form of Segner's recurrence: $C_{n+1}\,(n+2) = 2(2n+1)\,C_n$. Since $2(2n+1)/(n+2) \in (2, 4)$ for $n \ge 1$, this gives $2C_n \le C_{n+1} < 4C_n$, the discrete shadow of $C_n \sim 4^n/(n^{3/2}\sqrt\pi)$.

title: Bridge to the Central Binomial Coefficient and Positivity
content: `catalan_mul_succ` clears the division in Mathlib's `catalan_eq_centralBinom_div` using `Nat.succ_dvd_centralBinom` (that n+1 divides C(2n,n)), recovering Cₙ·(n+1) = C(2n,n) — matching the parent's identity but obtained directly from Mathlib primitives. `catalan_pos` deduces 0 < Cₙ from this bridge together with `Nat.centralBinom_pos`. These two facts are the only inputs the recurrence proof needs.
mathContext: $C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1)$ and $(n+1) \mid C(2n,n)$, so $C_n(n+1) = C(2n,n)$. Since $C(2n,n) > 0$ and $n+1 > 0$, also $C_n > 0$.

title: Segner's Recurrence C_{n+1}·(n+2) = 2(2n+1)·Cₙ
content: The core result. Applying the bridge at n and at n+1 gives C_{n+1}·(n+2) = C(2(n+1),n+1) and Cₙ·(n+1) = C(2n,n); Mathlib's `Nat.succ_mul_centralBinom_succ` supplies (n+1)·C(2(n+1),n+1) = 2(2n+1)·C(2n,n). Substituting both bridges into this and cancelling the common factor n+1 (via `Nat.eq_of_mul_eq_mul_left`) yields the recurrence. The whole proof is a linear substitution plus one cancellation.
prerequisites: cancellation of a positive factor in ℕ

title: Sharp Two-Sided Ratio Bounds
content: Because the recurrence multiplies Cₙ by 2(2n+1)/(n+2), which lies strictly in (2, 4) for n ≥ 1, the growth per step is bounded on both sides. `catalan_succ_lt_four_mul`: C_{n+1} < 4Cₙ (from 2(2n+1) < 4(n+2), cancelling the positive factor n+2 via `lt_of_mul_lt_mul_right`). `two_mul_catalan_le_succ`: 2Cₙ ≤ C_{n+1} for n ≥ 1 (from 2(n+2) ≤ 2(2n+1)). `succ_succ_dvd_two_mul`: n+2 divides 2(2n+1)Cₙ with quotient C_{n+1}, an immediate divisibility corollary. Each nonlinear step is discharged by `nlinarith` using positivity of Cₙ.
mathContext: For $n \ge 1$: $2 \le \dfrac{2(2n+1)}{n+2} < 4$, hence $2C_n \le C_{n+1} < 4C_n$. The divisibility $\,(n+2) \mid 2(2n+1)C_n\,$ holds because the quotient is the integer $C_{n+1}$.

title: Factorial-Free Computation
content: The closing example shows the recurrence computing C₅ from C₄ with no factorials: C₅·6 = 2·9·C₄, i.e. 42·6 = 252 = 18·14. This is the practical payoff — Segner's recurrence turns Catalan-number computation into a single multiply-and-divide per step, in contrast to the parent's additive definition (which needs two binomial coefficients) and its convolution recurrence (which needs a full sum).
